CHAPTER 3: THE IMPACT OF ROME (Section B, Part 2: The Vision of Jesus in Context)

BIG IDEA
- Jesus lived in first-century Palestine, an occupied country under Roman rule.
- For Jews, land and religion were closely linked: the land was God's gift and a sign of the covenant.
- Roman rule, and especially Roman polytheism and taxes, threatened Jewish monotheism and identity.
- This tension led to different Jewish groups - Zealots, Sadducees, Pharisees and Essenes - each responding to Rome in its own way.
- Opening quote: "Then they took Jesus from Caiaphas to Pilate's headquarters. It was early in the morning." (John 18:28)

KEY TERMS
- Covenant: the special agreement or relationship between God and the Jewish people (God's chosen people).
- Monotheism: belief in one God only. Judaism is monotheistic (Yahweh).
- Polytheism: belief in many gods. Imperial Rome was polytheistic.
- Political life: the structures of power and organisation of the Jewish State - who was leader, who made laws, the collection of taxes.
- Religious life: the faith and religious rituals of the Jewish people.
- Social life: how people lived together in society (family, community, Temple).
- Prefects: Roman governors appointed by the Emperor to rule the province of Judea.
- Procurator: another name for the Roman governor (prefect) appointed by Rome.
- Pontius Pilate: the Prefect of Judea at the time of Jesus.
- Sanhedrin: the 71-member High Council of the Jews, presided over by the high priest.
- Zealots, Sadducees, Pharisees, Essenes: the four main Jewish groups of the first century.
- Torah: the Law of Moses as recorded in the Holy Scriptures.
- Gentile: a non-Jew (e.g. a Greek or Roman).

THE PROMISED LAND - GOD'S PROMISE TO ABRAHAM
- Genesis 12:2-3: "I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you, and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing... in you all the families of the world will be blessed."
- The Promised Land was about four hundred miles south of Haran.
- From the beginning Jews saw the land as a gift from God and a sign of God's covenant with them.
- This belief that they were God's chosen people would have serious implications for paying taxes to Rome later.

MOSES AND THE EXODUS
- Story of Moses' birth and adoption by Pharaoh's daughter is well known.
- Exodus 3:7-10, the call of Moses: God says "I have observed the misery of my people who are in Egypt; I have heard their cry... I have come down to deliver them... to bring them up... to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey..." God sends Moses to Pharaoh to bring the Israelites out of Egypt.
- A series of events convinced the Hebrews of their chosen status.
- On Mount Sinai God made an everlasting covenant with Israel and gave Moses the Ten Commandments and the Law (Exodus chapter 19).
- Despite difficulties, the Israelites developed an identity as God's chosen people.
- This marked the definitive emergence of monotheism in Judaism - allegiance to one God only.

LIFE IN PALESTINE UNDER ROMAN RULE
- Judaism was challenged from within and without; the greatest threat from without was the Roman presence.
- Imperial Rome threatened the very survival of Judaism; the most fundamental threat was Roman polytheism.
- Land and religion were closely linked: the land and its produce belonged to God.
- Paying taxes to Rome would be unfaithful to God - they could not give to Caesar what belonged to God. God was their leader and king.
- Roman polytheism was in direct conflict with Jewish monotheism.
- The Jewish reaction to threats to monotheism deeply affected their political, religious and social life.
- So the first century was a time of tension; political and religious life could not easily be separated.

A HISTORY OF OCCUPATION
- Palestine had been influenced by the Persians, then the Greeks, and by the first century was part of the expanding Roman Empire.
- By the time the Romans came, the people were reeling from centuries of occupation; once again under foreign rule.
- Their sense of being God's chosen people was again under attack.
- Many groups emerged, each offering a way to hold on to what was important.

HOW ROME RULED PALESTINE
- 63 BCE: the Romans colonised Palestine.
- Roman policy: appoint native rulers where possible. Herod the Great was made king of the Jews. Jesus was born during his reign.
- 4 BCE: Herod the Great died; his kingdom was divided among his three sons.
- Herod Archelaus ruled Judea and Samaria - a difficult region. He was a tyrant who inspired great fear and could not manage the restless people.
- Jews and Samaritans pleaded with Rome to remove him. Rome deposed him and installed a Roman governor - the beginning of direct Roman rule.
- The southern area became the Roman province of Judea, governed by prefects appointed by the Emperor.
- At the time of Jesus, the Prefect of Judea was Pontius Pilate.
- Northern Palestine, Galilee, was ruled by another son, Herod Antipas - a "puppet" prince who took orders from Rome and collected Roman taxes from the Galileans.
- Jesus and John the Baptist lived in Galilee.
- Galilee was known for political unrest and considerable turmoil.
- The Prefect of Judea kept a close eye on Galilee and was especially wary of large religious gatherings in Jerusalem.

THE GOVERNMENT OF JUDEA
- Imperial Rome was polytheistic. The Emperor had divine status (considered a god); a cult grew up around this. This was completely alien to monotheistic Jews loyal to Yahweh.
- The high priest represented the people before God. He was Head of State but had little real power. He ruled and presided over the Sanhedrin.
- Structure: High Priest (Head of State) -> Sanhedrin (71-member High Council) -> Executive Committee (priests/laymen) -> Scribes/Pharisees (experts on the Law).
- The Roman prefect (procurator) could appoint and dismiss the high priest.
- Rome wanted peace and calm in this troublesome part of the Empire.
- The Sadducees were the most powerful group in the "government" and followed the path of least resistance.
- The Pharisees posed no threat to Rome and were free to follow the Law as long as they paid taxes.
- There was no place in the Sanhedrin for the militant, violent, subversive Zealots.

JERUSALEM IN THE TIME OF JESUS
- The Jews had a nomadic history, but by the first century had settled in large urban areas like Jerusalem.
- Traditional nomadic kinship (family) patterns disappeared.
- Jerusalem became the religious, political and cultural centre of Judaism, mainly because of the Temple.
- The Temple was the centre of religious, social and political life.
- The Law of Moses was the law of the land in Jewish understanding.
- The conflict between being a faithful Jew and obeying Rome led to several important groups emerging.

THE FOUR GROUPS - WHAT THEY SHARED AND HOW THEY DIFFERED
- Shared: a history, belief in the one true God, and the Law of Moses in the Torah.
- Differed: in interpreting the Law, attitude to the Romans, Temple rituals, and what they believed their covenant called them to do.
- They show the impact of Roman rule on social, political and religious life.
- With nomadic family ties gone, people looked to the Temple and religious leaders for guidance.

THE ZEALOTS - MILITANT RESISTANCE
- Radical, militant group; believed they must take an active part in delivering God's chosen people.
- Duty to oppose the Roman presence and struggle against anything that challenged the Jewish faith/state.
- Particular allegiance to the Maccabees and their revolt (164 BCE); drew on this history of violent resistance.
- Channelled fear and frustration into violence.
- May have appealed to those who suffered most under Rome, especially over taxes (economic injustice plus religious objection).
- Like subversive militant groups today, arose from injustice, fear and frustration.
- Little support for the view that Jesus was linked to the Zealots - his clear non-violent stance shows he was not one of them.
- No place for them in the Sanhedrin.

THE SADDUCEES - CO-OPERATION
- Mainly conservatives - opposed radical or sudden change.
- Much to gain from courting the Romans; they had held power and status before the Romans and were allowed to keep it by co-operating with the "enemy".
- Attracted the powerful and wealthy.
- Power and status were linked to the Temple, so many Sadducees were associated with Temple life.
- Co-operated with the Romans to survive; part of the puppet government that administered law and collected taxes.
- The most powerful group in the government; followed the path of least resistance.
- Risk: a cultural loss of identity. They did not survive into the twentieth century.

THE PHARISEES - STRICT OBSERVANCE OF THE LAW
- Fell between the Zealots and Sadducees: neither militant nor co-operative.
- Saw both other paths as threats: Zealots risked death (violent end); Sadducees risked cultural loss of identity.
- Believed survival came only through strict and absolute observance of the Law of Moses and its rituals, keeping Jewish identity distinct.
- Easily recognisable by their observance; e.g. keeping the Sabbath holy, rigorously upheld, which set a Jew apart from a Gentile (Greek or Roman).
- National identity safeguarded by strict observance of the Law.
- Posed no threat to Rome; free to follow the Law as long as they paid taxes. Scribes/Pharisees were the experts on the Law in the government structure.
- They get the most criticism in the gospels, but they were right that the Law was their means of survival - they survived and continue to. The Zealots and Sadducees did not survive into the twentieth century.

THE ESSENES - WITHDRAWAL
- Identified with the Qumran community.
- Evidence found in 1947 with the discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls.
- Marked by withdrawal from the world; a monastic type of group.
- Saw no way forward through politics or violence.
- Only way to be faithful to Yahweh: withdraw from the compromised world of first-century Judea and live a life of prayer and religious contemplation.
- Lived in strict isolation, awaiting a new age and God's intervention to bring a better world.

JESUS AND THE GROUPS
- No convincing evidence that Jesus belonged to any of these groups.
- He was aware of all of them and no doubt met each at different times.

SUMMARY TABLE (RESPONSE TO ROME)
- Zealots: fight (violent resistance).
- Sadducees: co-operate (keep power and status).
- Pharisees: keep the Law strictly (preserve identity).
- Essenes: withdraw (prayer and isolation, await God).

KEY DATES AND PLACES
- 164 BCE: Maccabean revolt.
- 63 BCE: Romans colonise Palestine.
- 4 BCE: Herod the Great dies.
- 1947: Dead Sea Scrolls found at Qumran.
- Places on the map: Jerusalem, Cana, Nazareth, river Jordan, Qumran, Sea of Galilee, Judea, Galilee, Dead Sea, Caesarea.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words why the Jews saw themselves as God's chosen people.
rows.model_answer: God promised Abraham he would make him a great nation and gave his people a land. God called Moses to free the Israelites from Egypt and lead them to a land flowing with milk and honey. On Mount Sinai God made an everlasting covenant with them and gave the Ten Commandments and the Law.

rows.prompt: Explain how Roman and Jewish religious beliefs were in direct conflict.
rows.model_answer: The Romans were polytheistic, believing in many gods, and even treated the Emperor as a god. The Jews were monotheistic and loyal to Yahweh alone. Paying taxes from God's land to Rome also felt like being unfaithful to God, who was their true king.

rows.prompt: What was the role of the prefect in first-century Palestine?
rows.model_answer: The prefect was a Roman governor appointed by the Emperor to rule the province of Judea. He could appoint and dismiss the high priest and kept a close eye on unrest, especially in Galilee and at large religious gatherings in Jerusalem. Pontius Pilate was prefect in Jesus' time.

rows.prompt: Describe how Herod the Great's kingdom was ruled after his death in 4 BCE.
rows.model_answer: It was divided among his three sons. Herod Archelaus ruled Judea and Samaria, but he was a tyrant and Rome replaced him with a Roman governor, beginning direct rule. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee as a puppet prince who collected Roman taxes.

rows.prompt: Explain the significance of the Temple for Jews in the first century.
rows.model_answer: The Temple made Jerusalem the religious, political and cultural centre of Judaism. It was the centre of religious, social and political life. Positions of power and status were linked to it, and people looked to it and their religious leaders for guidance on keeping the covenant.

rows.prompt: Describe the Sadducees and their attitude to Rome.
rows.model_answer: The Sadducees were mainly wealthy, powerful conservatives linked to the Temple. They co-operated with the Romans so they could keep their positions of power and status. They were part of the puppet government that administered law and collected taxes.

rows.prompt: Why does the chapter say the Pharisees were 'correct' in their belief about survival?
rows.model_answer: They believed the Jewish people would survive only through strict observance of the Law of Moses. They saw the Zealots' violence as risking death and the Sadducees' co-operation as risking a loss of identity. The Pharisees survived and continue to, while the Zealots and Sadducees did not.

rows.prompt: Describe the Essenes and their response to Roman rule.
rows.model_answer: The Essenes were a monastic type of group linked to Qumran, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found in 1947. They withdrew from the compromised world to live in strict isolation, in prayer and contemplation. They waited for God to intervene and bring a new age and a better world.

rows.prompt: Outline the way in which Rome governed Palestine in the first century. Refer to Judea, Galilee, prefects, Pontius Pilate and Herod Antipas.
rows.model_answer:
The Romans colonised Palestine in 63 BCE. Their policy was to appoint native rulers where possible, so Herod the Great was made king of the Jews; Jesus was born during his reign. When Herod died in 4 BCE his kingdom was divided among his three sons.

Herod Archelaus ruled Judea and Samaria. He was a tyrant who could not manage the restless people, and the Jews and Samaritans pleaded with Rome to remove him. Rome deposed him and installed a Roman governor, the beginning of direct Roman rule. The southern area became the Roman province of Judea, governed by prefects appointed by the Emperor. At the time of Jesus the Prefect of Judea was Pontius Pilate. The prefect could appoint and dismiss the high priest, who presided over the 71-member Sanhedrin.

Galilee in the north was ruled by Herod Antipas, a 'puppet' prince who took orders from Rome and collected Roman taxes. Jesus and John the Baptist lived in Galilee, a region of political unrest, so the prefect watched it closely and was wary of large religious gatherings in Jerusalem.

rows.prompt: Describe the response of two of the following groups to Roman rule in first-century Palestine: Zealots, Sadducees, Pharisees, Essenes.
rows.model_answer:
The Zealots were a radical, militant group. They believed they must take an active part in delivering God's chosen people and saw it as their duty to oppose the Romans and anything that challenged the Jewish faith or state. They had a particular allegiance to the Maccabees and their revolt of 164 BCE and channelled people's fear and frustration into violent resistance. They probably appealed to those who suffered most, especially from taxes, which were both an economic injustice and a religious offence. There was no place for them in the Sanhedrin, and Jesus' non-violence shows he was not one of them.

The Pharisees took a middle path. They rejected the Zealots' violence, which risked death, and the Sadducees' co-operation, which risked a loss of identity. They believed the chosen people could survive only through strict and absolute observance of the Law of Moses and its rituals. For example, they rigorously kept the Sabbath holy, which set Jews apart from Gentiles. They posed no threat to Rome and were free to follow the Law as long as they paid taxes. Though criticised in the gospels, they were right: they survived, while the Zealots and Sadducees did not.

May refer to: Zealots - militant, Maccabees 164 BCE, oppose Rome, taxes, not Jesus; Sadducees - conservative, wealthy, Temple, co-operate to keep power, puppet government, loss of identity; Pharisees - strict Law, Sabbath, identity, no threat to Rome, survived; Essenes - Qumran, Dead Sea Scrolls 1947, withdrawal, prayer, await new age.

rows.prompt: 'In first-century Palestine it was difficult to separate the political life of the Jewish people from their religious life.' Discuss.
rows.model_answer:
For the Jews, land and religion were closely linked. God had promised Abraham a land and made a covenant with Moses on Mount Sinai, giving the Ten Commandments and the Law. The land was seen as God's gift and a sign of the covenant, and its produce belonged to God. This shaped their identity as the chosen people and their monotheism - loyalty to one God only.

Roman rule challenged this directly. Rome was polytheistic and the Emperor was treated as a god, which was alien to the Jews. Paying taxes to Rome - a political matter - was a religious problem, because giving God's produce to Caesar seemed unfaithful to God, their true king.

The structures of government also mixed the two. The high priest, who represented the people before God, was Head of State and presided over the 71-member Sanhedrin, but the Roman prefect could appoint and dismiss him. The Law of Moses was the law of the land, and the Temple was the centre of religious, social and political life.

Finally, each group's political response to Rome came from its religious beliefs: the Zealots fought, the Sadducees co-operated, the Pharisees kept the Law strictly and the Essenes withdrew to wait for God.

May refer to: definitions of political and religious; land as gift and covenant; monotheism vs polytheism; Emperor cult; taxes; high priest, Sanhedrin, prefect; Temple as centre; Law of Moses as law of the land; groups' responses rooted in faith.

rows.prompt: Write a note on the significance of the Temple in the life of the Jewish people of the first century.
rows.model_answer:
The Jews had a history as a nomadic people, but by the first century many had settled in large urban areas like Jerusalem. The traditional kinship patterns of nomadic life disappeared, and Jerusalem became the religious, political and cultural centre of Judaism. More than any other single element, this was because of the Temple.

The Jewish people saw the Temple as the centre of religious, social and political life. With family ties weakened, the 'people of God' looked to the Temple and their religious leaders for guidance on how to be faithful to the covenant. Positions of power and status were directly linked to the Temple, which is why many Sadducees, the most powerful group in the government, were associated with Temple life. The high priest, who represented the people before God, presided over the Sanhedrin. The different Jewish groups also differed in their Temple rituals. Because the Temple drew large religious gatherings to Jerusalem, the Roman prefect was particularly wary of them.
